4. Engagement, observation, release and restoration

The introduced timing budget is:

Operation	Target time
Brush, scan, align and search	20 s
Set individual feet and source clamp	7 s
Proof, settle, inspect locks and transfer fixture	43 s
Total engagement and qualification	70 s
Supported release	20 s
Docked cleaning, inspection and reset	60 s

This gives 100 seconds of robot occupation and 150 seconds of controller operation, because 50 seconds of restoration occur in a paid independent dock.

The seven-second foot-setting allowance is particularly uncertain. Adjusting one foot changes the others through frame movement, so the tool must iterate and recheck after locking.

Actual observations

The shared tool needs:

A calibrated six-axis wrench measurement at the relevant geometry.
Local spring-compression measurements.
Independent returned-position witnesses for each bank.
Fixture-port and foot motion relative to the wall.
Images of contact condition, particles and local damage.
Force and travel records during engagement and release.

The proposed disc stack has a tangent stiffness of roughly 0.9–1.1 kN/mm. Inferring an individual foot force within ±5 N therefore requires approximately ±4–6 µm total installed spring-compression accuracy. That includes hysteresis, calibration and temperature; camera pixel size is insufficient.

After the tool removes its normal support, the sum of the four foot forces must close against the drawbar force and external normal load. This helps reject a drawbar loaded against an internal stop while providing little wall clamp.

A proof curve still does not predict every future crack. The relation between the observed state and 24-hour survival must be validated on the declared surfaces.

Release has three distinct support jobs

The service tool must separately:

Take the useful fixture load.
Carry the head’s own weight.
Capture the internal normal and radial preloads.

Only then may locks move and the banks reverse.

Zero external wrench does not mean the cancelling radial forces have disappeared. Each bank’s stored force needs a measured unload path.

The 10 N separating-force limit is measured on the normal release stage. A real cradle carries the head’s approximately 14.7 N weight; that weight is not removed by a numerical tare.
